sittings.bodyEn: A marketing professor asks which single advantage you would want for a hot dog stand. Students offer location, quality, low prices, and taste until they run out of answers. His answer is a starving crowd. A bad hot dog, a bad price, and a bad corner can still sell out if you are the only stand when a college game lets out. Early in a health crisis, toilet paper sold at extreme prices with no crafted offer and no clever pitch, because people were desperate. When demand is that strong, a mediocre operator with a weak offer and weak persuasion can still make money.

terms.hook: A market so hungry that a plain offer can still sell out.

sittings.bodyEn: Lloyd's software let newspapers add a digital ad product in a few clicks, and he charged only a share of the new revenue. If they made nothing, he made nothing, so the offer put the risk on him, and he could sell. The business still declined, because newspapers were shrinking about 25 percent a year. He had checked the product, the offer, the selling, and the team, and the market was the piece he faced last. When mask demand exploded, he started an automated factory, got the unit cost under the import price, and was doing millions a month within five months. Same person and a trade he did not know, with a crowd that urgently wanted the product.

terms.hook: A shrinking pool that fights you even when the product, the offer, and the selling are strong.

sittings.bodyEn: He tells owners to drop the romance and serve people who can pay what the work is worth. You need demand, and the job is to channel it into your offer. Inventing demand is a different and harder job, and this book assumes a market already exists. A normal market, in his usage, grows about as fast as the wider marketplace and has an unmet need in health, wealth, or relationships. Lloyd could have applied every later chapter to newspapers and still failed, because that market was shrinking. A normal market is enough for serious money, and selling ice where ice is already everywhere is his picture of a market with no hunger.

terms.hook: Growing about as fast as the wider world, with an unmet need in health, wealth, or relationships.
Point hunger that already exists toward your offer.

sittings.bodyEn: The first of four market tests is massive pain: they need the result, and mild interest is too weak. Pain can be broken finances, a bad marriage, a long line, a bad back, a smile they dislike, or extra weight. The price you can charge rises with how severe the pain is, which the value chapter unpacks. When they hear the pain stated clearly, and the life without it, they lean toward the solution. He trains sales teams with a short line: the pain is the pitch. Good writing helps a reader understand, and good persuasion helps a prospect feel understood.

terms.hook: A problem they desperately need solved, which supports a higher price.
Say their pain accurately and they move toward the offer.

sittings.bodyEn: A friend had a strong system for improving resumes so people landed more interviews. He still could not get paid. The buyers were unemployed. Pain, a large crowd, and a steady stream of new people had fooled him into calling it a great market. The missing test was purchasing power. The audience needs the money, or access to the money, at a price that makes your time worth spending.

terms.hook: The buyer can pay the price that makes the work worth your time.

sittings.bodyEn: A perfect market you cannot find will never see the offer. He looks for people who already gather: associations, mailing lists, social groups, and channels they all watch. If reaching them feels like hunting scattered needles, the offer stays invisible. Wanting to serve wealthy doctors is workable, because they can be found. Showing the promotion to nursing students means the message misses those doctors, however strong the offer is. This test is practical: the ads have to reach the people the offer was built for.

terms.hook: The buyers already gather somewhere you can advertise.

sittings.bodyEn: A growing market is a tailwind, and a shrinking market is a headwind. Newspapers had pain, purchasing power, and an easy way to reach them. They were still shrinking fast, so the whole marketplace pushed against the effort. That missing fourth test was Lloyd's real problem. Business is already hard, and markets move quickly. Choose a market that pushes the work forward.

terms.hook: A tailwind: the pool is getting larger, so the same effort goes further.

sittings.bodyEn: Health, wealth, and relationships keep producing demand because lacking them hurts. Inside one of those, find a smaller group that is growing, can pay, and is easy to reach. A relationship guide will do better with people in the second half of life than with college couples. Older people who are alone often feel sharper pain, have more money, and are easier to find. At the time of writing, more people were turning 65 each year than turning 20, so that group was also growing. Start from a skill you already have in one of the three markets, then choose the people who value it most, as long as their market is stable or growing.

terms.hook: The three lasting markets, because the pain of lacking them never disappears.

sittings.bodyEn: The order of importance is the starving crowd, then the strength of the offer, then persuasion skill. Rate each one great, normal, or bad. A great score on a higher lever overpowers a weak score below it, a normal score passes the question downward, and a bad score stops you unless a great score above it covers the hole. Hot dogs outside the bars at closing time sell to a hungry crowd even with a bad offer and weak persuasion. In a normal market, a grand slam offer can make a lot of money even if you are a weak closer, and that reader is who this book is for. A normal market plus a normal offer requires exceptional persuasion, which is a real path and the longest one.

terms.hook: Market first, offer second, persuasion third.

sittings.bodyEn: He uses the phrase niche slap for owners who pick a market and then refuse to stay. One quiet test that fails to produce a million is weak evidence that the market is bad. Dentists and chiropractors are both normal markets with huge revenue, and either can work. Trying to serve both at once breaks the commitment, because the rule is to pick one. Every market has unpleasant parts, and hopping niches restarts the failures from the beginning. Try a hundred offers and one can succeed: a failed offer means the offer failed, and the person fails when they stop trying.

terms.hook: The reminder to stay in the market you picked until the offer is actually tested.

sittings.bodyEn: Under $10,000,000 a year, a tighter niche usually makes more money, and past that it depends on the total addressable market, because you can only grow as far as that pool. Many firms passed $30,000,000 inside one niche, including chiropractors, gyms, plumbers, solar, roofers, and salons, so being at $1,000,000 or $3,000,000 is a reason to get better at the current niche. Broaden later by going up market, down market, or into a neighbor where the same service still helps. His gym offer spoke only to a small-gym owner with about 100 members, a signed lease, at least one employee, and a goal of helping clients lose weight, and he turned away trainers and online coaches so the message stayed sharp. A generic time-management course might be $19, the same ideas for salespeople about $99, for outbound business sellers about $499, and for outbound sellers of power tools and garden gear $1,000 to $2,000, because one extra deal can cover the fee. A fat-loss plan for everyone at $19 and a plan for shift nurses near $2,000 can share the same core habits, and the specific buyer pays more because it feels made for them. A free checklist for scoring a market sits with the training videos if you want to mark a niche against pain, money, reach, and growth.

terms.hook: The full pool you can serve, which caps how far that niche can grow.
The same core can sell for far more when the buyer believes it was built for them.

sittings.bodyEn: This chapter gives four tests before you build the offer. A market can pass three and still fail if the fourth is missing, as the newspapers did. Passion for a hobby is a separate fact from these tests. Choose the four signs he uses.
sittings.prompt: Which four signs does this chapter use to judge a market?
choices: Deep pain, money to pay, a way to reach them, and a market that is growing
A clever name, a low price, a long guarantee, and a famous founder
The largest audience you can name, even when they cannot pay and the trend is shrinking
A personal hobby, a discount, a viral post, and a rival's price list
